title: Waymo Sensor Fusion Processor at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Waymo disclosed its in-house Sensor Fusion Processor, a 208 mm2 N5 chip in a 45x45 mm FCBGA package under 75W with in-package LPDDR5x at 273 GB/s, 160 INT8 TOPS, 64 MB of on-chip SRAM, and a carTPU array running camera, radar, and fusion backbones. Waymo positions it as the first purpose-built ASIC for autonomous driving at scale, already running in sixth-generation vehicles.

themes.theme: Vertical integration of autonomous driving silicon

insights.claim: Waymo has moved beyond off-the-shelf autonomous driving accelerators to silicon co-designed around its own sensor fusion models, putting it in control of the entire sensor-to-embedding path.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Removes a merchant-silicon supplier from the AV stack and raises the capital bar for competitors relying on third-party AV chips.
insights.quote: Waymo has moved beyond off-the-shelf autonomous driving accelerators to silicon co-designed around its own sensor fusion models.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: Waymo positions the carTPU as the first purpose-built ASIC for autonomous driving at scale, co-designed from the ground up, and notes riders can experience it in sixth-generation vehicles.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Silicon already in a live fleet rather than on a roadmap, which is the difference between an announcement and a competitive fact.
insights.quote: Waymo closes the sensor fusion talk by positioning the carTPU as the first purpose-built ASIC for autonomous driving at scale.
insights.locator: Waymo closes the sensor fusion talk

insights.claim: Waymo designed the carTPU, ISP, codecs, and MIPI ingest path with scratchpad memory in house, while sourcing two GPUs, the on-chip interconnect, memory, PCIe and Ethernet controllers, PHYs, secure boot, and peripherals from third parties.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows the build-versus-buy line a systems company draws when it enters silicon: differentiating datapath in house, commodity IP licensed.
insights.locator: Major subsystems split between Waymo-designed and proven third-party IP

insights.claim: Waymo deliberately excluded DSPs from the design, partly due to the required programming skills.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Engineering talent availability, not silicon efficiency, drove a major architectural exclusion, a constraint that applies broadly to custom silicon programs.
insights.quote: Notably, Waymo does not have DSPs in this. They said it is partly due to the required programming skills.
insights.locator: Major subsystems split between Waymo-designed and proven third-party IP

insights.claim: The Sensor Fusion Processor fits in a 45 mm by 45 mm FCBGA package with 208 mm2 of silicon on an N5 process, pairing in-package LPDDR5x at 273 GB/s with a PCIe Gen5 x8 host interface, 25G Ethernet, and a TDP of less than 75W.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A sub-75W, 208 mm2 leading-edge part sets the realistic power and area budget for in-vehicle AI, far below data center accelerators.
insights.quote: This part fits in a 45 mm by 45 mm FCBGA package with 208 mm2 of silicon on an N5 process, pairing in-package LPDDR5x memory at 273 GB/s with a PCIe Gen5 x8 host interface, 25G Ethernet, and a TDP of less than 75W.
insights.locator: Headline specifications are compact for the class

insights.claim: Waymo quotes 160 TOPS for INT8 by INT8 and 80 TFLOPS for FP16 with 64 MB of on-chip SRAM, an 8 MB register file, and 160 GB/s of external memory bandwidth, saying it is focused on higher precision to preserve fidelity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Choosing precision over headline TOPS runs against the industry's FP4 race and reflects safety-critical fidelity requirements.
insights.quote: Waymo quotes 160 TOPS for INT8 by INT8 and 80 TFLOPS for FP16, with 64 MB of on-chip SRAM, an 8 MB register file, and 160 GB/s of external memory bandwidth.
insights.locator: Compute throughput relies on integer and higher-precision

insights.claim: Waymo can run liquid cooling in vehicles sitting in the Phoenix summer sun but with 60C liquid, a very different thermal regime from the data center.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 60C liquid inlet caps achievable in-vehicle silicon power, explaining why automotive AI compute will lag data center density indefinitely.
insights.quote: they can have vehicles sitting in the Phoenix summer sun that have liquid cooling, but with 60C liquid which is very different than in the data center
insights.locator: Waymo wants in-house sensor processing co-designed

insights.claim: Waymo measures latency from first pixel in to embedding out at low batch sizes, rather than optimizing throughput at large batch.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Batch-1 latency is the metric that separates real-time embedded AI from data center serving, and it invalidates data center benchmark comparisons.
insights.quote: with latency measured from first pixel in to embedding out at low batch sizes
insights.locator: Waymo wants in-house sensor processing co-designed

insights.claim: The carTPU architecture pairs a control block with a core array of 16 processing elements and 2 cores, with each control PE field carrying a dual-core RISC-V CPU with vector extensions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: RISC-V in a shipping safety-critical AV product is a meaningful commercial validation of the ISA outside microcontrollers.
insights.locator: This architecture overview shows a control block

insights.claim: Waymo relies on deterministic mega-instructions with static shapes, running single-thread execution over roughly a thousand cycles with no caching or branches, using FIFOs and memory with semaphores for ordering and backpressure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Removing caches and branches makes latency provably deterministic, which is a safety-certification requirement general-purpose accelerators cannot meet.
insights.quote: Waymo relies on deterministic mega-instructions with static shapes, running single-thread execution over roughly a thousand cycles with no caching or branches
insights.locator: Dataflow principles keep the hardware lean

insights.claim: Each processing element keeps a highly banked 2 MB SRAM sized so activations and context stay resident to feed GEMVs, with ring and mesh DMA dividing weight streaming from cross-PE collectives and a 4x compute slice sustaining INT8 GEMV per cycle with sparse gather and scatter fusion.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sizing SRAM to hold the working set entirely on chip is how Waymo avoids the memory bandwidth wall that dominates data center inference.
insights.locator: Each processing element keeps a highly banked 2 MB SRAM

insights.claim: Waymo's software follows a compiler-first philosophy where ahead-of-time compilation builds a mega-kernel for the whole model and shards it to fit in SRAM, leaving the compiler to manage partitioning, global memory traffic, race conditions, and numerical accuracy.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Pushing complexity into the compiler is what lets the hardware stay simple and deterministic, a reusable pattern for embedded AI silicon.
insights.quote: Ahead-of-time compilation builds a mega-kernel for the whole model and shards it to fit in SRAM
insights.locator: Software follows a compiler-first philosophy

insights.claim: Waymo argues achieved performance matters more than raw TOPS, plotting continuous optimization as relative speedup against initial latency to show co-design and measured efficiency beating headline throughput.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the TOPS-based marketing that dominates automotive AI chip comparisons.
insights.quote: Waymo argues that achieved performance matters more than raw TOPS here.
insights.locator: Waymo argues that achieved performance matters more

insights.claim: Waymo's carTPU cores split across three backbones for camera, radar, and fusion, with the fusion path latency-critical while camera and radar backbones run at maximum concurrency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Different optimization targets per backbone show why a single general-purpose accelerator is a poor fit for the AV workload.
insights.locator: Waymo’s carTPU cores split across three backbones

insights.claim: Waymo builds its own demosaic rather than using a standard image signal processor block, because traditional demosaic can introduce zipper and color artifacts while the in-house version preserves color accuracy and edge detail.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Image-processing artifacts propagate into model inputs, so ISP quality is a perception-safety issue rather than a photography one.
insights.quote: Waymo builds its own demosaic rather than using a standard image signal processor block.
insights.locator: Waymo builds its own demosaic

insights.claim: The camera pipeline produces a YUV pyramid with sub-frame latency roughly a few hundred image lines behind sensor read-out, with MIPI ingest outputs progressing as the ISP advances as far as it can.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sub-frame pipelining is the mechanism that removes whole-frame buffering latency, a direct contributor to vehicle reaction time.
insights.quote: the YUV pyramid is produced with sub-frame latency roughly a few hundred image lines behind sensor read-out
insights.locator: Pipelining keeps the camera flow moving

insights.claim: Patch extraction pulls arbitrarily scaled regions of interest from the YUV pyramid, converts color space, and applies synthetic HDR exposure so models only see the windows they need.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Feeding models only relevant windows cuts compute per frame, an efficiency lever unavailable to generic vision accelerators.
insights.locator: Patch extraction follows in the camera path

insights.claim: Multi-frame temporal denoising trades latency for cleaner images, which matters at night and in low-contrast settings for downstream fusion.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A concrete latency-versus-accuracy trade the AV system must tune, and one that shapes night-driving capability claims.
insights.locator: Temporal denoising compares a single-frame result

insights.claim: HDR sensing targets headlight glare at night and the transition out of a tunnel, both of which drive the dynamic range requirements the chip must meet.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Names the specific edge cases that set sensor and ISP specification floors for any AV program.
insights.locator: HDR sensing targets the hard real-world cases

insights.claim: A GPU stage handles point cloud processing, waveform processing with FFT cubes, and GPGPU programming models separately from the carTPU inference cores.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Splitting signal math onto GPUs and inference onto the ASIC is a heterogeneous partitioning pattern other embedded AI systems are likely to copy.
insights.locator: A GPU stage handles the heavy sensor math

insights.claim: Some radar and lidar data takes an Ethernet path directly to the host, offloading traffic from the GPU and carTPU so sensor math and model inference do not compete for the same bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Bandwidth contention, not compute, is a first-order design constraint in multi-sensor systems.
insights.locator: Some radar and lidar data takes an Ethernet path

insights.claim: Typical radar processing is built on multi-dimensional FFTs producing range, Doppler, and azimuth projections that feed the point and feature representations later fused with camera data.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Explains why AV silicon needs strong FFT throughput alongside matrix math, a requirement general AI accelerators do not address.
insights.locator: Typical radar processing is built on multi-dimensional FFTs

insights.claim: Waymo's foundation-model stack routes camera, lidar, and radar embeddings into a sensor fusion encoder that this silicon was built to run, while the driving VLM handles higher-latency-tolerant tasks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The latency-tolerance split between encoder and VLM is the architectural reason a dedicated encoder ASIC pays off.
insights.quote: The driving VLM is more for the higher-latency-tolerant tasks.
insights.locator: Today’s focus is the sensor fusion encoder

insights.claim: Waymo traces its AI evolution from deep convolutional networks in 2013 through transformers and large datasets to a foundation-model stack driving perception, planning, and world modeling by 2024, which is the reason it built its own silicon.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Model architecture convergence on transformers is what made a fixed-function ASIC viable; unstable model architectures would have made it a bad bet.
insights.locator: An evolution timeline explains why Waymo built its own silicon
